facts.statement: The fossil skeleton of Inkayacu includes fossilized feathers, representing the first known feathers preserved in any penguin.
facts.quote: It includes fossilized feathers, the first known in penguins.

facts.statement: Analysis of melanosomes in Inkayacu feathers indicates the bird had gray or reddish-brown plumage.
facts.quote: A study of the melanosomes, pigment-containing organelles within the feathers, indicated that they were gray or reddish brown.

facts.statement: The genus name Inkayacu translates to "Water Emperor" or "king of the water" from Quechua words.
facts.quote: The genus name derives from the Quechua words Inka for emperor or king and yacu for water, thus the name translates to "Water Emperor" or, more idiomatic, "king of the water".

facts.statement: The species name paracasensis refers to the Paracas region where the fossils were discovered.
facts.quote: The specific epithet, paracasensis, refers to Paracas, where the fossils were found.

facts.statement: Inkayacu was among the largest fossil penguins, measuring 1.5 meters long and weighing between 54.6 and 59.4 kilograms.
facts.quote: Inkayacu was among the largest described fossil penguins, measuring 1.5 m long and weighing about 54.6 - 59.4 kg, twice as heavy as the average emperor penguin, the largest extant penguin.

facts.statement: Fossils of Inkayacu were first found in 2008 on the Pacific coast of Ica, Peru.
facts.quote: Fossils of Inkayacu were first found in 2008 on the Pacific coast of Ica, Peru.

facts.statement: The skeleton was uncovered from the Otuma Formation in the Paracas National Reserve by an expedition led by Rodolfo Salas and studied by a team led by Julia Clarke.
facts.quote: A nearly complete skeleton was uncovered from the Otuma Formation, in the Paracas National Reserve by an expedition team led by Rodolfo Salas and studied by a team led by Julia Clarke of the University of Texas.
It was nicknamed, "Pedro," by the researchers that had discovered it.

facts.statement: The well-preserved feathers allowed researchers to perform an analysis of melanosomes.
facts.quote: The feathers were well enough preserved that researchers Julia Clarke, Liliana D'Alba and Ali J. Altamirano were able to perform analysis of melanosomes.

facts.statement: Inkayacu inhabited the seas of Peru during the Late Eocene.
facts.quote: Inkayacu inhabited a sea that existed in Peru during the Late Eocene.

facts.statement: Inkayacu's paddle-like limbs enabled an aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Paddle-like limbs enabled an aquatic lifestyle.

facts.statement: It is debated whether modern penguin melanosomes provide an underwater advantage, as their white undersides lack melanin rigidity.
facts.quote: However, it is also possible that the melanosomes of modern penguins do not give them an advantage underwater, since the feathers on their undersides are primarily white, lacking the rigidity of melanin.

facts.statement: Inkayacu is classified as a genus of extinct penguins.
The only species within the genus Inkayacu is I. paracasensis.
The genus Inkayacu was described by Clarke et al. in 2010.
Inkayacu lived between 37.71 and 33.9 million years ago during the Priabonian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Priabonian to Priabonian (37.71 to 33.9 million years ago)
